title: Chapter 22 — Merry Christmas
paragraphs: At length, toward noon, after the ship's riggers were finally dismissed, and after the Pequod had been hauled out from the wharf, and after the ever-thoughtful Charity had come out in a whale-boat with her last gifts — a nightcap for Stubb, the second mate and her brother-in-law, and a spare Bible for the steward — after all this, the two captains, Peleg and Bildad, emerged from the cabin. Turning to the chief mate, Peleg said:
"Now, Mr. Starbuck, are you sure everything is ready? Captain Ahab is all set — just spoke to him — nothing more to get from shore, eh? Well, call all hands, then. Gather them aft here — blast them!"
"No need for profane words, however great the hurry, Peleg," said Bildad. "But off with you, friend Starbuck, and carry out our orders."

How about that! Here at the very moment of departure, Captain Peleg and Captain Bildad were running the show on the quarter-deck, just as if they were going to be the joint commanders at sea as well as, to all appearances, in port. As for Captain Ahab, there was still no sign of him. They said he was in the cabin. But the idea was that his presence wasn't at all necessary for getting the ship underway and steering her well out to sea. That was really the pilot's job, and since he hadn't fully recovered — so they said — Captain Ahab stayed below. All of this seemed natural enough, especially since in the merchant service many captains never show themselves on deck for some time after the anchor is raised, but stay at the cabin table having a farewell party with their shore friends before those friends leave the ship for good with the pilot.
But there wasn't much time to think it over, because Captain Peleg was now fully energized. He seemed to do most of the talking and commanding, not Bildad.
"Get back here, you sons of bachelors!" he cried, as the sailors lingered at the mainmast. "Mr. Starbuck, drive them aft."

"Strike the tent!" was the next order. As I mentioned before, this whalebone shelter was only set up in port. Aboard the Pequod, for thirty years, the order to strike the tent was well known to be the step right before raising the anchor.
"Man the capstan! Blood and thunder — jump!" was the next command, and the crew sprang for the handspikes.

Now, when getting underway, the pilot usually stations himself at the front of the ship. And there was Bildad, who — along with Peleg, you should know — was one of the port's licensed pilots in addition to his other roles. He was suspected of having got himself licensed just to save the Nantucket pilot fee for every ship he had a stake in, since he never piloted any other vessel. Bildad, I say, could now be seen looking over the bow for the approaching anchor, and at intervals singing what seemed a dismal verse of a psalm to cheer the men at the windlass. They roared out some sort of chorus about the girls in Booble Alley, with hearty good will. This despite the fact that not three days before, Bildad had declared that no profane songs would be permitted aboard the Pequod, especially while getting underway. And Charity, his sister, had placed a small, choice copy of Watts, the hymn-writer, in each seaman's berth.

Meanwhile, overseeing the other end of the ship, Captain Peleg raged and swore astern in the most frightful manner. I almost thought he'd sink the ship before the anchor could be raised. I involuntarily paused at my handspike and told Queequeg to do the same, thinking of the dangers we faced in starting a voyage with such a devil for a pilot. I was comforting myself with the thought that pious Bildad might offer some salvation, despite his seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay, when I felt a sudden sharp jab in my rear. Turning around, I was horrified to see Captain Peleg withdrawing his leg from my immediate vicinity. That was my first kick.

"Is that the way they heave in the marchant service?" he roared. "Spring, you sheep-head; spring, and break your backbone! Why don't you spring, I say, all of you — spring! Quohog! Spring, you fellow with the red whiskers; spring there, Scotch-cap; spring, you green pants. Spring, I say, all of you, and spring your eyes out!" And with that, he moved along the windlass, using his leg very freely here and there, while the imperturbable Bildad kept leading off with his psalm-singing. Captain Peleg, thinks I, must have been drinking something today.

At last the anchor was up, the sails were set, and off we glided. It was a short, cold Christmas Day. As the brief northern daylight merged into night, we found ourselves nearly out on the wintry ocean, whose freezing spray coated us in ice like polished armor. The long rows of whale teeth along the bulwarks gleamed in the moonlight. And like the white ivory tusks of some enormous elephant, vast curving icicles hung from the bow.

Gaunt Bildad, as pilot, headed the first watch. And again and again, as the old ship plunged deep into the green seas and sent shivering frost everywhere, and the winds howled, and the rigging sang, his steady voice could be heard:
"Sweet fields beyond the swelling flood, Stand dressed in living green. So to the Jews old Canaan stood, While Jordan rolled between."

Never did those sweet words sound more beautiful to me than at that moment. They were full of hope and fulfillment. Despite this frigid winter night on the wild Atlantic, despite my wet feet and even wetter jacket, it seemed to me there were still many pleasant harbors ahead — meadows and glades so eternally springlike that the grass that shot up in the spring remains, untrodden and unwilted, at midsummer.
At last we reached such a distance from shore that the two pilots were no longer needed. The sturdy sailboat that had accompanied us came alongside.

It was curious, and not unpleasing, how Peleg and Bildad were affected at this point, especially Captain Bildad. For, loath to depart just yet, very loath to leave for good a ship bound on so long and perilous a voyage — beyond both stormy Capes; a ship in which some thousands of his hard-earned dollars were invested; a ship in which an old shipmate sailed as captain, a man almost as old as himself, setting out once more to meet all the terrors of the pitiless jaw; loath to say goodbye to a thing so brimful in every way of every interest to him — poor old Bildad lingered long. He paced the deck with anxious strides; ran down into the cabin to speak another farewell word there; came on deck again and looked to windward; looked toward the wide and endless waters, bounded only by the far-off, unseen Eastern Continents; looked toward the land; looked aloft; looked right and left; looked everywhere and nowhere; and at last, mechanically coiling a rope on its pin, he convulsively grasped stout Peleg by the hand and, holding up a lantern, stood for a moment gazing heroically into his face, as much as to say, "Nevertheless, friend Peleg, I can stand it; yes, I can."

As for Peleg, he took it more philosophically. But for all his composure, there was a tear glistening in his eye when the lantern came too close. And he, too, kept running from cabin to deck — a word below, then a word with Starbuck, the chief mate.

But at last he turned to his companion with a final sort of look about him. "Captain Bildad — come, old shipmate, we must go. Back the main yard there! Boat ahoy! Stand by to come alongside now! Careful, careful — come, Bildad, old friend — say your last. Good luck to you, Starbuck. Good luck, Mr. Stubb. Good luck, Mr. Flask. Goodbye and good luck to you all — and three years from today, I'll have a hot supper waiting for you in old Nantucket. Hurrah and away!"

"God bless you, and have you in His holy keeping, men," murmured old Bildad, almost incoherently. "I hope you'll have fine weather now, so that Captain Ahab may soon be moving among you — a pleasant sun is all he needs, and you'll have plenty of that on the tropic voyage you're making. Be careful in the hunt, you mates. Don't stave the boats needlessly, you harpooners; good white cedar plank has gone up a full three percent within the year. Don't forget your prayers, either. Mr. Starbuck, mind that cooper doesn't waste the spare staves. Oh! The sail needles are in the green locker! Don't whale it too much on the Lord's days, men; but don't miss a fair chance either — that's rejecting Heaven's good gifts. Keep an eye on the molasses cask, Mr. Stubb; it was a little leaky, I thought. If you touch at the islands, Mr. Flask, beware of fornication. Goodbye, goodbye! Don't keep that cheese too long down in the hold, Mr. Starbuck; it'll spoil. Be careful with the butter — twenty cents a pound it was, and mind you, if —"
"Come, come, Captain Bildad — stop chattering — away!" And with that, Peleg hurried him over the side, and both dropped into the boat.

Ship and boat parted ways. The cold, damp night breeze blew between them. A screaming gull flew overhead. The two hulls rolled wildly. We gave three heavy-hearted cheers and plunged blindly, like fate, into the lonely Atlantic.
